Sam Loyd's Son's Dissection

ParadoxesAreaSequences
Game: A square of 64 cells is cut into four pieces that seem to make a shape of only 63 cells. Where did a cell go?
How to play: Drag the pieces into the dashed shape, or press the buttons or Animate. Then try Cheat and other sizes.
Look for the math

The pieces are the same as in the famous trick where an 8 × 8 square seems to make a 5 × 13 rectangle. Here they go together differently: a 5 × 5 block, a row of 13, and another 5 × 5 block, which counts 25 + 13 + 25 = 63 cells. Cutting and moving pieces cannot change their area, so something must be wrong.

Two slopes that are almost equal

The long slanted line of the figure is made of two cuts: the triangles' long side climbs 3 cells in 8, a slope of 3/8 = 0.375; the trapezoids' slanted side climbs 2 in 5, 2/5 = 0.4. They are so close that the eye sees one straight line, but they are not, and along that line the pieces overlap. The overlap has area exactly 1: the 64 cells of the pieces squeeze into 63.

Fibonacci numbers and Cassini's identity

3, 5, 8, 13 are consecutive Fibonacci numbers, and Size picks other runs of them. For a square of side F with neighbours E before and G after, the figure has 2E² + G·(2D − E) cells, where D comes before E. By Cassini's identity this is always one more or one less than F²: 25 against 26, 64 against 63, 169 against 170, 441 against 440. When the figure is smaller the pieces overlap; when it is larger they leave a thin gap. The logic test checked every size the applet offers: the pieces always tile the square exactly, and the figure is always off by one. On the smallest size, 3 × 3, the middle row has no thickness at all and the pieces visibly do not fit.

Cheating

As the page says, this dissection paradox shows its flaw more than the 64 = 65 one. With Cheat on, the applet nudges one corner of each piece (by a fifth of a cell and a thirteenth of a cell for 8 × 8) so the slopes match and the overlap almost disappears. Those pieces no longer have the area they had in the square.

Put the pieces in with Cheat off and look closely where the two triangles meet the trapezoids. Then try 13 × 13: where is the extra cell now?
